11145-the-discovery-of-yellowstone-park-:
Nathaniel Pitt Langford published this 1905 journal of the Washburn Expedition to the Yellowstone and Firehole Rivers in 1870. Langford opens with James Bridger, discoverer of Great Salt Lake, a mountaineer fond of practising on listeners' credulity. Bridger, asked about his long life on the plains, pointed at Pumpkin Butte near Fort Laramie and replied that the mountain was a hole in the ground when he came.

Bridger, in the Rockies since 1820 and a partner in the Rocky Mountain Fur Company by 1832, spent months far from settlements, living on roots for bread. Langford, who met him in 1866, records the expedition's daily travel: by six votes to three the party went around Yellowstone Lake, passed steam rising from hot springs. The journal is a founding document of Yellowstone's discovery.
12030-the-spectator-volumes-1-2-and-3-wi:
Henry Morley's three-volume edition of The Spectator, published in 1891, reproduces the original text both as first issued and as corrected by its authors, with introduction, notes, and index. Morley, professor of English literature at University College, London, presents Addison and Steele's famous periodical in a scholarly but readable form.

The Spectator's essays, on manners, literature, morals, and daily life in early eighteenth-century London, created the essay periodical as English readers knew it. Morley's edition, priced at ten shillings and sixpence per set of three, lets a modern reader follow the papers in order. Its notes explain persons, places, and allusions that time had made obscure.
13960-charles-rex:
Ethel M. Dell published Charles Rex in 1922, a romance of power, pride, and love. Charles, a strong and magnetic figure, dominates a Mediterranean world of terraces, cypress trees, and sea views. He feels ancient and dilapidated one night, pausing on steps to look over the water. Women, rivals, and old sins test his rule.

Dell opens with verse on half-gods giving way to gods, and on sin, success, pleasure, and gold. Charles must learn humility before love can save him. The novel mixes passion, melodrama, and moral judgment in Dell's usual manner. Its setting adds glamour to the conflict. Readers of Dell will find her full romantic force here.
14969-three-contributions-to-the-theory-:
Sigmund Freud's Three Contributions to the Theory of Sex, in the Nervous and Mental Disease Monograph series, appears here in a second edition, second reprinting, translated by A. A. Brill with an introduction by James J. Putnam. Freud divides the work into sexual aberrations, infantile sexuality and the transformation of puberty.

Each essay argues that sexual life begins in childhood, develops through stages and can take many forms, challenging Victorian silence. Brill, of Columbia and Bellevue, gives American readers a direct translation, while Putnam frames it for physicians. The book is a landmark of psychoanalysis, now read as history of ideas as much as science, and its terms still shape talk about desire.
15015-sex-and-society-studies-in-the-soc:
William I. Thomas, associate professor of sociology at the University of Chicago, gathers studies in the social psychology of sex, published by the University of Chicago Press in 1907 and reprinted in 1913. The studies first appeared in journals at different times and were revised and expanded for this volume.

Each study stands complete in itself, yet a general thesis runs through all of them, linking sex, custom and social life. Thomas writes as an early sociologist, observing how societies shape desire, courtship and family roles. The book is a landmark of American sociology, now read for its method and its period views as much as for its conclusions.
16266-harvard-psychological-studies-volu:
Hugo Munsterberg edited volume one of Harvard Psychological Studies, published by Macmillan as a bi-monthly record of the Harvard lab for mind study. It contains sixteen lab tests, brought together because lab results had spread in various places or stayed unpublished for lack of space. From now on, the preface says, the Studies will publish Harvard lab work more fully and in one place.

Only pieces from lab members appear, giving the volume a focused, sober tone. Early lab work in mind study, with its tools, reaction times, and sense tests, fills its pages. Students of mind study's history will find a key set from America's leading lab of the day.
20696-highways-and-byways-in-sussex:
Highways and Byways in Sussex is a travel book in the beloved Highways and Byways series, which walked readers county by county through England. Its Sussex volume crosses the Downs, the coast towns, and the weald between. Anecdote and history season every mile of the road.

The Downs give Sussex its unique character, the writer says. Their virginal security and unassailable independence set them apart. They stand, a silent undiscovered country, between the seething pleasure towns of the seaboard plain and the trim estates inland. The book teaches readers to see that quiet country as its lovers did.
22328-oh-you-tex:
William MacLeod Raine wrote Oh, You Tex!, a western novel of the open desert. Its hero, Jack Roberts, starts the story fifty miles from nowhere. Alone, he dances to a tin cup beaten against a tin plate.

Youth, Raine writes, set his feet to moving. Jack is twenty-one, five feet eleven, and solidly built. He carries one hundred seventy pounds of bone, sinew, and muscle. That cheerful opening tells readers what kind of hero to expect. Raine filled westerns with riders, ranches, and quick action. Tex gives that formula a likable start, with a young cowboy happy even in empty country.
2300-the-descent-of-man-and-selection-in:
Charles Darwin's Descent of Man applies evolution to humanity itself, arguing that people share ancestry with other primates. The book marshals evidence from anatomy, behavior, and fossils, then turns to sexual selection: how mate choice shapes plumage, antlers, song, and display across species. Darwin writes carefully, aware of the storm his claims would raise.

The work's second half ranges across birds, insects, and mammals to show selection at work in courtship. Its Victorian language on race and gender now reads as dated, but its core argument reshaped biology. The book remains essential for understanding Darwin's full theory.
23308-the-white-feather-hex:
Don Peterson wrote this short weird tale, first printed in Weird Tales in the early nineteen fifties. Peter Scheinberger, a strong Pennsylvania Dutch farmer with arms like knotted hickory, works weather-beaten hills where old folk beliefs still hold power.

A white feather turns red as a sign of a hex at work, and the farm's fate hangs on breaking the spell. Peterson's tale mixes rural realism with folk horror, and it shows the pulp magazine's taste for curses close to home. Rain beats on the slate roof while Mirestone sits by the fire with the Dutchman, a question hanging unsaid.
24397-hex:
Larry M. Harris wrote this story, with pictures by Summers, for Astounding Science Fiction in May 1959. Its blurb introduces Gloria, a worker for the Welfare Department who likes helping people, only she really-but-good helps them. Gloria's office is not bright or sunny, but that does not matter. If she wants sun, she can tune in on a mind outside, someone walking New York streets. What matters is how you feel inside.

Gloria, twenty-one and eager, crams her beret into a drawer at ten minutes to nine, facing reports and folders. Neatness is the keystone of good work, so she spends twenty minutes ordering everything, though the cleaning woman, she thinks, upset it. Mr. Fredericksohn arrives around nine-thirty, but the case workers are ready, and Gloria beams, glad to help people and to know she is right. Readers get a telepath on the welfare rolls.
25533-history-of-the-english-people-inde:
John Richard Green supplies the index to his History of the English People in this 1896 volume, part of the Eversley edition of a work first issued in 1879. Readers use it to find people, places, and events across all eight volumes, with volume and page numbers for each entry.

Entries run from Archbishop George Abbot and Abelard through generals, princes, abbeys, sieges, and political slogans such as the Abhorrers. For a long history without a single narrative thread, the index is the working tool that lets a reader trace one person or town through centuries.
26295-the-printer-boy-or-how-benjamin-fr:
William M. Thayer's Printer Boy, issued in London by James Hogg and Sons, tells Benjamin Franklin's early life as an example for youth. Its preface states its maxim plainly: the boy is father to the man. Franklin's childhood runs to his start in business, with his manhood achievements summed up in a closing chapter.

Thayer writes actual life as story, mixing narrative and dialogue in the manner of Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress. Readers meet the whistle bargain, in which young Franklin learns the price of wanting too much, and his debates with Collins, which pushed him toward a strict plan of self-culture. The book aims to make industry, thrift, and study attractive to young readers.
28518-mex:
William Logan's short story Mex is told by a seventeen-year-old boy near the Mexican border, on the American side. Men drinking in a bar spit on him and call him Mex, as if being Mexican were something to hide or be ashamed of. The boy answers back with names of his own.

Held back by other men as he lunges at a big red-haired bully, the boy threatens that his sister, a witch, will curse his tormentors. He boasts that his father is a giant ten feet tall. Logan's quiet story turns on pride, insult, and ancestral memory, and on a boy caught between anger and the wish to make things right.
29046-the-heads-of-apex:
Francis Flagg wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Astounding Stories in October 1931. Its hero, Justus Miles, sits hungry and desperate on a park bench when wind blows a newspaper advertisement to his feet. It wants a soldier of fortune, young and healthy, with good credentials, at 222 Reuter Place. Miles, a veteran of the World War, Kemal's Turkey, the Riffs in Morocco, and filibustering in South America, answers the call.

A note promises adventure far under the sea floor. There, Solino's submarine will carry two American soldiers of fortune among the vampire heads of Apex. Flagg writes pulp adventure with a straight face, mixing want ads with undersea horror. Readers get a brisk 1930s tale of a down-and-out soldier hired for a strange voyage, and the wonders waiting below.
29250-historic-court-memoirs-of-france-a:
David Widger edited this index volume to the Project Gutenberg Historic Court Memoirs of France series. Rather than a single memoir, the volume gathers and indexes a whole shelf of French court memoirs, with chapter lists and illustrations for each. It serves as a guide to the series.

The memoirs indexed include Marguerite de Valois, Queen of Navarre, Cardinal de Retz, Madame de Montespan, the Duchess of Orleans on Louis XIV and the Regency, and Saint-Simon. Later volumes cover Louis XV and XVI, Marie Antoinette by Madame Campan, the court of St. Cloud, and Count Grammont. Readers get a map to centuries of French court life, useful for finding a reign, a writer, or a scandal.
29430-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-hal:
David Widger's index to the works of Hall Caine gathers the Manx novelist's tales in one short file. It lists The Manxman, The Little Manx Nation, Capt'n Davy's Honeymoon, The Drama of 365 Days, Recollections of D. G. Rossetti, The Scapegoat, The Christian, The Eternal City, The Shadow of a Crime, A Son of Hagar, and The Woman Thou Gavest Me.

The index itself adds no new fiction; it gathers Caine's varied books so readers can find a title at once. From Manx shore tales to city melodrama and war writing, the range is wide. For lovers of popular Victorian and Edwardian fiction, it is a neat map of a once-famous storyteller's shelf.
29431-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-raf:
David Widger compiled and edited this index to the Project Gutenberg works of Rafael Sabatini. The index does not reprint the novels; it links each title to its source file, with full contents listed, so readers can jump straight to a book. A click on any title, the contents promise, takes the reader instantly to that file.

Titles indexed include Mistress Wilding, Captain Blood, Scaramouche, and Historical Night's Entertainment in two parts. St. Martin's Summer, The Snare, and Trampling of the Lilies follow. So do The Life of Cesare Borgia, Love-at-Arms, and The Sea-Hawk. The Shame of Motley, The Strolling Saint, and The Suitors of Yvonne appear too. The Tavern Knight, Bardelys the Magnificent, and The Lion's Skin complete the list. Readers get a finding aid to a swashbuckling novelist's shelf.
29434-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-fla:
David Widger compiled and edited this index to the Project Gutenberg works of Flavius Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian. The index lists Josephus's works in volumes, so readers can find a text and its table of contents without hunting through the catalogue. It is a guide, not a history itself.

Volumes indexed include Against Apion, Concerning Hades, and the Life of Flavius Josephus. The two great histories follow. The Antiquities of the Jews traces Jewish history from creation to the eve of revolt. The Wars of the Jews is Josephus's account of the revolt against Rome. Readers get a compact map to Josephus, whose works remain the chief source for first-century Judea outside the Bible.
29441-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-pla:
An index by David Widger gathers the dialogues of Plato that have shaped Western thought. Its contents list Apology, Crito, Phaedo, Critias, Charmides, Laches, Lysis, and The Republic. Eryxias, Theaetetus, Timaeus, Meno, Alcibiades I and II, Cratylus, Protagoras, Statesman, Gorgias, Ion, Menexenus, Lesser Hippias, and Phaedrus follow, each linked to its full text.

The index adds no new philosophy; it maps Plato's whole shelf in one short file. Readers can move from Socrates on trial to the ideal city, from love to law, without hunting title by title. For students of ancient thought, it serves as a clear, complete guide to the dialogues in the Gutenberg set.
29459-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-xen:
David Widger compiled this short index to the Project Gutenberg works of Xenophon, the Greek soldier and writer who marched with the Ten Thousand and wrote of Socrates. It lists the texts in the set: Anabasis, Hellenica, Cyropaedia, Memorabilia, the Apology, works on horsemanship, hunting, revenues, and the polity of Athens. Each title stands as a doorway to a full text in the same series.

The index itself holds no new prose by Xenophon; its worth lies in gathering his varied works in one place. Readers can move from war memoir to Socratic talk to tracts on farm and state without hunting title by title. For students of Greek prose, it serves as a neat map of a wide and still readable ancient author.
29467-the-project-gutenberg-works-of-jos:
David Widger compiled this index to the Project Gutenberg works of Joseph Crosby Lincoln, the Cape Cod novelist beloved for his tales of old seamen and shore folk. It lists Keziah Coffin, The Depot Master, Thankful's Inheritance, Cy Whittaker's Place, Cap'n Eri, Mary-'Gusta, Shavings, Cape Cod Stories, and more, with verse in Cape Cod Ballads. Each entry points to a full text in the same series.

The index adds no new fiction of its own; it maps a whole shelf of Lincoln's work in one short file. Readers can pick a harbor tale, a village comedy, or a ballad set without hunting title by title. For lovers of Cape Cod stories and period dialect humor, it is a handy guide to a warm, bygone shore world.
29896-sex-the-unknown-quantity-the-spiri:
Ali Nomad, whose name covers Dr. Alexander J. McIvor-Tyndall, published Sex: The Unknown Quantity in Chicago in 1916, with the Sterling Publishing Company. The subtitle promises a new and startling reading of the meaning, scope, and function of sex, seen from the inner or cosmic standpoint. It claims to present a practical solution to the sex problems of everyday life. The book is dedicated to the child of tomorrow, the man-god whom we await.

The publisher's foreword calls the work an epoch in advanced thought and human evolution, and says no earlier book on sex was at once so illuminating, convincing, and satisfying. Those are the publisher's claims, not settled facts, and the book should be read as a period occult work. Its author was already known for Cosmic Consciousness and books on ghosts, thought, and the hand.
31006-the-author-s-printing-and-publishi:
Held here is an 1839 guide for authors, The Author's Printing and Publishing Assistant, published in London by Saunders and Otley of Conduit Street and printed by W. Blatch of Grove Place. Its full title promises explanations of the process of printing, preparation and calculation of manuscripts, choice of paper, type, binding, and illustrations, and publishing and advertising. It adds an exemplification of the typographical marks used in correcting the press.

Its contents run from the process of printing and its origin and progress through stereotype, copper plate, and wood engraving. They continue with preparation and calculation of manuscript, choice of paper and type, correcting the press, typographical marks, illustrative engravings, choice of binding, and publishing and advertising. It opens by noting that authors, and those who give directions to a printer, should know how printing is performed. It is a practical handbook from the hand-press age.
31749-the-irish-ecclesiastical-record-vo:
This alphabetical index covers volume one of The Irish Ecclesiastical Record, a monthly journal conducted by a society of clergymen under episcopal sanction and published at Dublin by John F. Fowler in 1865. Its motto, taken from the sayings of Saint Patrick in the Book of Armagh, runs in Latin and in English: as you are children of Christ, so be you children of Rome.

Entries range from the See of Achonry and the See of Ardagh to saints' feasts, prayers, tombs, and articles on eternal punishment, the Bible, and letters of bishops and cardinals. Readers get a finding aid to a year of Irish Catholic journalism, useful for tracing people, places, and debates of 1865.
32492-endless-amusement-a-collection-of-:
Endless Amusement, from the seventh London edition and published in Philadelphia in 1847, collects nearly four hundred entertaining experiments in many branches of science. Its subjects include acoustics, electricity, magnetism, arithmetic, hydraulics, mechanics, chemistry, hydrostatics, and optics, with wonders of the air-pump and all popular tricks and changes of the cards. A complete system of pyrotechny, or the art of making fireworks, is added.

The whole is explained so clearly, the title page promises, as to suit even the most limited capacity. Index entries range from convertible aces and aeolipiles to electrified bubbles, magic bells, and paper balloons loaded with stars and serpents for fireworks. Readers get a hands-on Victorian science book, full of parlour experiments, card tricks, and firework recipes.
32937-women-in-all-ages-and-in-all-count:
Rénald Lévesque's index volume serves a ten-volume illustrated series, Women in All Ages and in All Countries. The series was issued in a limited edition de luxe of one thousand numbered copies. The series moves from Greek women and Roman women through women of early Christianity and the Orient. It goes on to women of medieval France, the romance countries, modern France, and the Teutonic nations. Each volume is by a scholar of its field.

This index gathers that whole sweep into one usable guide, letting a reader find a figure, a period, or a theme across all ten books without hunting volume by volume. It is a reference tool rather than a narrative. Its value lies in the range it opens: ancient, medieval, and modern women treated as subjects of history in their own right. For research into the series, it is the key volume.
38162-practical-religion-being-plain-pap:
Practical Religion, by John Charles Ryle, bears the subtitle Plain Papers on the Daily Duties, Experience, Dangers, and Privileges of Professing Christians. This edition comes from the Baker Book House of Grand Rapids, Michigan. Ryle writes in short, direct papers meant for ordinary believers rather than scholars.

Twenty-one chapters cover the Christian's daily ground. Self-Inquiry opens the book, taking Paul's proposal to revisit the churches and see how they do as its text. Prayer, Bible-Reading, Going to the Table, Charity, and Zeal follow, with warnings against formality and the world. Riches and Poverty, Sickness, The Family of God, and Our Home lead toward Heirs of God, The Great Gathering, The Great Separation, and Eternity. Ryle's plain papers were among the most read devotional books of his century.
39499-moores-fables-for-the-female-sex:
Moore's fables, addressed to the female sex and embellished with engravings, appear here in a London edition of 1806. The first fable, The Eagle and the Assembly of Birds, is dedicated to the Princess of Wales. In his verses Moore promises truth under fiction: to weed out folly from the heart and show the paths that lead the wandering nymph astray from wisdom's way.

His targets are named in the prelude: the proud, the envious, and the vain, the jilt, the prude. With a friendly hand he holds the glass to all who pass, and if folly sees her likeness there, he made it not, but would amend. The fable of the birds turns on libels, factions, and a magpie who swears that magpies were never known to prate. Polite satire, dressed as a bird parliament.
39672-how-to-make-an-index:
How to Make an Index is a practical manual by Henry B Wheatley, published by Elliot Stock of London in 1902. The book is part of The Book-Lover's Library, which Wheatley edited. He had already written How to Catalogue a Library and How to Form a Library.

In 1878 Wheatley wrote a pamphlet, What is an Index, as the Index Society's first publication. He says the present book works on similar lines with a more practical aim. The first four chapters are historical, and the other four are practical. History shows what to imitate and what to avoid. A chapter on the bad indexer disproves the old idea that anyone can index without training. Wheatley admits the book leans on his own long experience. Details that may seem small are given on purpose.
40623-private-sex-advice-to-women-for-yo:
R B Armitage, a doctor of medicine, wrote this advice book for young wives and women about to marry. The Defiance Publishing Company of New York printed it, with a 1917 copyright. He states his aim at the front: to give light to those entering wedlock, so that married life may hold happiness and pleasure. The book is built as lessons.

Lesson one argues for sane teaching on the body and its sex life. It blames false lore from foul sources and an old taboo, traced to the Middle Ages, for much marital discord. Lesson two turns to anatomy in plain, scientific terms. Ovaries, ova, ovulation, puberty, and the change of life all get their due in the contents.
42494-the-paston-letters-a-d-1422-1509-v:
The Paston Letters, 1422 to 1509, close with this index part. Volume Six splits into two texts, letters and index. James Gairdner's edition runs to six volumes in all. Volume One, the general intro, came last of all. That matched the print order, a note says. This part starts at page 237 of the scan.

One index lists the letters and their titles. It names each writer and each person written to. Letter numbers guide that list, not pages. A general index gives volume and page for each name. Some See references were misspelled in print. Fixed forms sit in double brackets beside them. A list of faults waits at the text's end. Family letters from old Norfolk gain a key here that lets readers track five hundred papers by name.
42879-the-oriental-republic-of-uruguay-a:
The Oriental Republic of Uruguay at the Worlds Columbian Exhibition is a state book made for the great fair at Chicago in eighteen ninety-three. Its themes are the earth of the land, its farm crafts, its trade, and its broad counts. Two hands made it, one the head of the state count desk. A third hand put it in English dress.

A note from the last day of the past year owns that the facts rest in the main on the year past two. Full counts for the fair year were not yet to be had, since the count sheet comes out in the next year but one. Time was short and the stuff at the desk had to serve. The desk head had in truth made most of it past, so the work was a swift set in order of his store.
43036-the-life-of-william-ewart-gladston:
The Life of William Ewart Gladstone Index supplies the index for the three volume life of the Victorian prime minister. Entries run in alphabetical order and point readers to volumes one, two, and three. Each entry packs sub entries into a chronicle of acts, speeches, and ties. Lord Aberdare appears as home secretary in 1868 and in the Collier affair. His entry notes the licensing bill and the last cabinet meeting of 1874.

The Earl of Aberdeen entry covers different ground. It lists a Canada meeting, an estimate of Peel, and the Don Pacifico case. It also tracks the Crimean War talks, Gladstone's budget, and a letter to Prince Albert. Later lines note the Divorce bill, the Conspiracy bill, and debate on the Ionian project. The entry ends with Aberdeen's death and judgments of each man by the other.
43100-tex:
Clarence Mulford wrote a west tale of Tex and his gun fast road. A plate shows his gun leap to life at a snake's sight. Mulford wrote Hopalong Cassidy and the Bar 20 books. This book came out in March 1922 in New York. The Trail Calls leads its list of parts in firm style.

Fresh thoughts of old days and a new lure fill the front. A full day, a cheat cheated, and kind care come next. Weights and weights' tales, dark acts, and a fine ride build it. Speed and guile, bare praise, and close ties mark the mid arc. Out-cheat the cheats and tact with grit stand in the list. A good Samaritan and Buffalo Creek's glare close it. West fans get Mulford's hand.
46445-the-library-of-work-and-play-guide:
The Library of Work and Play Guide and Index is the key book to a ten book set of craft and home lore for the young. A note at its front tells that the set can be found whole in the free web shelf. It names each part of the set and its hand.

Carpentry and wood work come first, then the spark and its day uses. Garden and farm work, home dress, and house keep fill the mid run. Bench craft in and out of doors, needle work, games of the open air, and work in metals close the list. A front plate shows a boys own wire room, with most of its gear made at home or at school. The guide sums each book and points its parts.
46839-the-heart-of-wessex:
Sidney Heath described and E W Haslehust pictured The Heart of Wessex, in the Beautiful England series. Blackie and Son issued the book at London, Glasgow, and Bombay. A front picture shows Dorchester from the meadows.

Heath calls the region the country made famed by Thomas Hardy in his tales of rural life. For most uses, he says, Hardy's Wessex matches the county of Dorset. Hardy himself explained why he revived the old name Wessex in eighteen seventy-four. One county, Hardy found, gave too small a canvas for his plan. Plates show Puddletown, Bere Regis, Weymouth, and Corfe Castle. Hangman's Cottage at Dorchester and Poole Harbour also appear.
47185-schenk-s-theory-the-determination-:
Leopold Schenk, professor at the University of Vienna and director of its Embryological Institute, wrote The Determination of Sex, issued in an authorised translation by the Werner Company in 1898. Schenk's theory promised that a child's sex could be determined before birth, chiefly through the mother's diet and condition. The first chapter lays the groundwork in embryology.

Sex differences, Schenk writes, appear early in the embryo, in the exterior form and in the inner rudiments of the genital organs. For a time no investigation can distinguish them. He argues that the ovule itself carries the force that settles the question, passing it to the cells from which the organs develop. The book made Schenk famous and controversial across Europe and America. Later science discarded the theory, but the volume remains a document of the age's faith that biology would yield to management.
51362-lex:
W T Haggert wrote this short story, printed in Galaxy Magazine in August 1959 with art by Wood. Its hook is a sharp one: few men are as glad as a man who loves his work, but what happens when the work loves him back? Peter Manners, broke and close to eviction, goes to a job interview at Lex Industries.

Clay, at the engineers' guild, set up the meeting and warned him that the boss had turned down every man sent so far. Peter waits outside the plant to kill time. The place looks odd: plain walls, one small street door, and a loading bay set four feet off the ground. Something about the plant does not add up.
53289-the-restless-sex:
The Restless Sex is a novel by Robert Chambers, published in New York in 1918 by A L Burt by arrangement with Appleton. Chambers was the author of Barbarians and The Girl Philippa. A mock preface, part jest and part creed, opens the book before the story starts.

The preface says the restless sex, meaning woman, invented man as a helper and then invented gods in man's image. It ends by bringing on a little girl who should not have been born, being unwanted. She is the child of Harry Quest, a touring actor of no morals, and a young girl named Conway who tints photographs in Utica. The child starts life, the author warns, as heiress to obscure traits from both parents. What she turns into is left, he says, for time alone to solve.
53791-philosophical-works-v-1-of-4-inclu:
Volume One of the Philosophical Works of David Hume is a gathered edition of his writings in four volumes. It was printed at Edinburgh for Adam Black and William Tait in 1826. A portrait of Hume stands at the front of the volume.

The opening notice tells how the edition was made. Hume's writings are here gathered in one uniform set for the first time. The essays are reprinted from the edition of 1777, the last one Hume corrected for the press a short time before his death. He wished that edition to be taken as holding his thought. The editor has kept faithfully to that text. At the same time he has checked the earlier editions one by one.
53792-philosophical-works-v-2-of-4-inclu:
Philosophical Works of David Hume, volume two of four, is an Edinburgh edition of 1826. Adam Black and William Tait printed the set there, with Charles Tait in London. The edition includes all the essays, as its title page announces for the set. It exhibits the more important alterations and corrections in the successive editions published by the author.

Contents of this volume open with the Treatise of Human Nature, book two, Of the Passions. Part one treats pride and humility, their objects and causes, and the relations of impressions and ideas. Heads follow on vice and virtue, beauty and deformity, property and riches, and the love of fame. The edition belongs to the years when Hume, long suspect for his religion, was settling into the canon of British philosophy in print. Students still meet the Treatise in the shape this collected edition helped to fix.
56616-the-canadian-horticulturist-volume:
The Canadian Horticulturist, volume one, is the first year book of that farm sheet, out in eighteen seventy-eight. A fruit guild of the north land put it out, past a named shape hand. This file holds its full list and word list. Its prints run past the year in count rows, each with past six heads on fruit, bloom, and plot work.

Heads of the first print treat the sheet it self, a new grape, a cold half meet, and blooms of the far east. A warn to peach men of the north stands in that row. Next prints treat new pears and apples, the ills of apple trees, graft work past old plots, and the plum pest. Rose heads, meet notes, and grape flea trials fill the late rows.
57640-two-men-a-romance-of-sussex:
Two Men, a romance of Sussex by Alfred Ollivant, was published at Garden City, New York, in 1919. Ollivant wrote Bob, Son of Battle and The Gentleman. A motto calls necessity the spring of faith and mould of character. The book is dedicated to Beachbourne and the friends he made there from 1901 to 1911. Six books of chapters structure the long tale.

Heads name Beau-Nez, the Caspar family, and two brothers, Alf and Ernie. Ernie goes for a soldier, serves in India, and returns a changed man. Later books bring Ruth Boam, a Captain Royal who lays siege to a heart, and a quest. School, lash, church, and war shape two lives in Ollivant's warm, earnest prose.
58651-wessex:
Wessex is a travel book by Charles Harper in the Beautiful Britain series, dated 1911. Adam and Charles Black of London issued the volume with Sherborne abbey as frontispiece. Contents begin at Wareham and Bere Regis, out on the heaths of Dorset. Corfe Castle and Swanage follow, then Woolbridge House and Weymouth along the coast.

Under the Greenwood Tree country brings Dorchester, Maiden Castle, and Bridport into the tour. Cerne Abbas, the Vale of Blackmore, Sherborne, and Shaftesbury fill the fifth chapter. Cheddar cliffs, Wells, Glastonbury, and Bath close the circuit of the old kingdom. Hardy country walkers gain a pictured guide to the west of England.
5982-eeldrop-and-appleplex:
T. S. Eliot pairs two odd lodgers who rent small rooms in a disreputable part of town. Eeldrop and Appleplex come at nightfall, sometimes sleep, cook oatmeal, and leave in the morning for destinations unknown to each other. More often they talk or look out of the window.

They chose their street with care, preferring an evil neighborhood of silence to one of noise. A cloud of respectable concealment hangs over the curtained windows, while a police station across the way holds their gaze. Eliot turns their watching into a dry, unsettling comedy of manners.
59984-a-letter-to-john-wilkes-esq-sherif:
A Letter to John Wilkes, Esq; Sheriff of London and Middlesex is Robert Holloway's exposé of legal abuse. S Bladon printed it in London in 1771. Holloway was a gentleman of Gray's Inn. His subtitle promises detection of sheriffs' officers' extortion and oppression. The infamous practice of attornies is pointed out. A remedy is proposed for grievances the common people groaned under.

Holloway's address to the public refuses the usual flattery. He took chambers in Gray's Inn, he says, for one purpose. That purpose was detecting the abuses in his treatise. Retaliation followed swiftly. His furniture, books, and papers were seized under pretence of debt. A more flagrant pretence of execution dispossessed him of his rooms. He promises his pen will serve as faithful amanuensis to truth. Wilkes, the radical sheriff, is the letter's chosen patron. Considerations on the policy of arrests in general close the argument.
61690-saints-in-sussex:
Sheila Kaye-Smith wrote these verses on the saints for her own county of Sussex. Elkin Mathews printed Saints in Sussex in 1923, in a run of just 250 copies. This copy is number 131 of that small set.

A calendar of feasts frames the poems: Andrew, Philip and James, Peter and Paul. Mary Magdalene, Matthew, Ascension Day, and Pentecost follow. Corpus Christi, the Conception, and Lady Day in Harvest close the roll. The Andrew poem opens with Sussex men crying after the saint. What of the North, they ask, as he marches to the Picts. Stay and hear the little Southern men, they plead, in their shaggy forest land of Anderida.
63497-medicina-gymnastica-or-a-treatise-:
A medical treatise by Francis Fuller, printed at London in 1705. Robert Knaplock published the second edition, with additions. Its full title promises the power of exercise for the animal economy. The College of Physicians' censors approved the discourse. Their signed judgement, dated February 1705, stands in front.

Fuller's preface attacks a narrow idea of physic. Most men confine medicine to internals, he complains. Yet diseases enter by many doors, so health needs many roads back. Fluids and solids depend on each other, he argues. Each has its own disorders and its own proper applications. A violent seizure in one solid part draws all the rest into consent. Exercise, applied universally, can cure where local topics fail. The book helped found the medicine of movement.
68397-masters-of-the-vortex:
Masters of the Vortex is a science fiction novel by Edward Smith, first called The Vortex Blaster. The book appeared in 1960, and Smith dedicated it to Robert Heinlein. The tale belongs to the Lensman world, Smith's most famous creation. Its hero is Storm Cloud, the one man who can destroy wild atomic storms.

Loose nuclear storms strike and kill at random across settled space. Cloud hunts their source in a ship that is itself a flying arsenal. His crew is a band of colourful castaways from many worlds. A criminal mastermind crosses his path more than once. New sciences grow out of the hunt for the storms' cause. The blurb promises a final finding that shakes the fate of the universe. Smith writes space opera on the grand scale.
75130-tex:
Tex is a memoir of Alexander Teixeira de Mattos by Stephen McKenna, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead in 1922. A note warns that the chapter numbering is as printed: there is no Chapter Eight and no Chapter Twelve. McKenna dedicates the book to Alfred Sutro, who knew their friend the longer. A Stevenson letter on bereavement stands at the front.

Little of Tex, McKenna grants, has been made public. His love of laughing at himself, and his modesty and humour, would have been perturbed by fame. The book grew from reading his letters again. In them McKenna found a whim of language or an echo of laughter that recreated, for a moment, the triple alliance Tex founded. Teixeira de Mattos was the great translator of Dutch and French books into English. His Life and Letters never came; this slight, fond chapter stands in their place.
76051-the-strike-of-a-sex:
George Noyes Miller, a member of the Oneida Community, wrote this novel, issued at London by Reeves as number twelve of the Bellamy Library. His preface of January 1891, written from West Houston Street, New York, tells how he put the book forth in fear of women's verdict. He was answered by letters of gratitude from women in two continents.

A special preface to the English edition ties the tale to Malthus on population and Darwin on evolution. Its discovery, the preface claims, solves the population problem, the eugenic problem, social purity, and personal health in matters of sex. Miller asks when the primeval curse of brutalizing labour will be lifted from woman as from man. Chapter one finds the narrator drowsy on the road when a town of spires, domes, and busy chimneys appears close at hand. He enters its residence streets alert to a strange city.
76836-the-common-sense-of-sex:
James Oppenheim wrote The Common Sense of Sex, Little Blue Book Number One Thousand Eighty Nine, edited by E Haldeman Julius. The Haldeman Julius Company at Girard, Kansas, holds copyright in nineteen twenty six. Sex is a natural thing, and learning it has been one of the hardest lessons of this generation, Oppenheim opens. Christianity frowned on sex though granting it needful, he says.

A wave of revolt sweeps the western world, he notes. Walt Whitman praised sex as a clean, strong thing in verse. Havelock Ellis gathered a mine of information on the subject. Freud made a scientific study of sex and gave new light on its mysteries, he adds. Yet most folk stay in ignorance, hedged by fears, taboos, and shame, Oppenheim holds. Men and women of strong desires think they live in sin. Plain readers get a frank, cheap tract.
76872-tragedies-of-sex:
Tragedies of Sex gathers four plays by Frank Wedekind in English, with translation and introduction by Samuel Eliot. The volume was printed at New York by Boni and Liveright, with copyrights of 1914, 1921, and 1923. A warning at the front guards all stage and film rights in the plays under the laws of many lands.

The plays are Spring's Awakening, called a children's tragedy, Earth-Spirit, Pandora's Box, and Damnation. Spring's Awakening opens the book, with its schoolboys of fourteen to seventeen, their parents, and a faculty of grotesque doctors. Wedekind's plays, once banned and fought over, treat youth, desire, and ruin with a frankness that shocked their first audiences and reshaped modern drama.
77518-what-is-an-index:
What Is an Index is a set of notes on indexes and their makers by Wheatley. He was a fellow of a learned guild. He kept the funds of a guild for old texts, and was clerk of the index guild. It came out at London for that guild in the late eighteen seventies.

This is its second form, printed in a shire town. A quote at its head makes its case with zeal. A famed pen there holds the man who first made indexes in awe. He knows not to whom to give the palm. Is it the first great carver of the frame of man? Or the hid toiler who first laid bare the nerves of a book?
britannica-1911-convex: Convex is a term for the outer side of a curved or rounded surface. It stands opposed to concave, which names the inner side of such a surface. The word comes from Latin parts meaning with and to carry, or carried round. The Latin word for concave joins parts meaning with and hollow. In plain use, a convex surface bulges outward toward the viewer. A concave surface curves inward, away from the viewer, like a hollow.
britannica-1911-cromwell-thomas-earl-of-:
Thomas Cromwell, earl of Essex (about 1485–1540), was the only son of Walter Cromwell of Putney, a brewer, smith, and fuller. The son is said to have fled his father and served as a soldier in the French army in Italy. He fought at the Garigliano in December 1503 and was befriended at Florence by the banker Frescobaldi. He next appears at Antwerp as a trader. About 1510 he won papal indulgences for a Boston guild by a timely gift of sweetmeats to Julius II.

By 1512 Cromwell was in London, working as merchant and solicitor. The entry then traces his climb into the royal service of Henry VIII. Its closing bibliography shows the trail of that career. For the years from 1522 it rests on the Letters and Papers of Henry VIII and on Cavendish's Life of Wolsey. It also points readers to Merriman's Life and Letters of Thomas Cromwell, published in 1902.
britannica-1911-essex:
Essex, an eastern county of England, is mapped in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cambridge and Suffolk bound it north, the North Sea east, and the Thames south. London and Hertfordshire bound it west. Its area is one thousand five hundred and forty two square miles.

The lay of its rivers shows the shape of the land. Most streams are small. They run south and east to the Thames or to the sea. They reach the sea through broad, flat mouths that branch through low coast land. A few heads of streams in the north west drain north to the Cam. The high ground thus lies in the north west of the county. One long ridge runs south between two river paths. The entry gives the frame on which the rest of the county account is built.
britannica-1911-hastings-sussex:
Hastings is a borough town and sea resort in Sussex, England, one of the old Cinque Ports. It lies south east of London on two rail lines. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age, over sixty five thousand souls.

The town sits in a fine spot at the mouth of two thin vales. Hills to the north and east shield it, and give it a mild air of note. A broad walk fronts the sea and links it to a west suburb that lies in the borough. That part is chiefly a place of homes, with rail stops of its own. Both parts have fine piers, and a large park with lawns and trees was laid out in the past age. The sand beach is wide and famed for safe bathing.
britannica-1911-imbrex: Imbrex, the Latin word for a tile, is a building term explained in a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In the roofs of the ancient world, the plain flat tile was turned up on each side, and the imbrex was the covering tile laid over the joint between them. In the simpler kind of roof the imbrex is half round. In some Greek temples it has straight sides and a sharp, angled top instead.
britannica-1911-middlesex:
Middlesex, a county in the south-east of England, is surveyed in a long place entry in the 1911 Britannica. Save for Rutland it is the smallest county in England, at 283 square miles. The Thames forms its south edge, and the Lea parts it from Essex. The article deals chiefly with the part outside London. High ground runs along the north edge, past Stanmore and Harrow.

Much of the county was once thick forest and thinly peopled, a past kept in the name Enfield Chase. By the time of writing, London had spread its reach over near the whole county. Villages had grown into suburbs, and rail lines brought fresh ground to builders. The entry works through the rivers Brent, Crane, and Colne, the low flat land by the Thames, and the rocks below the soil. It pictures a rural county turning urban.
britannica-1911-narthex:
Narthex is a 1911 Britannica article on a part of the church building. The word is the Greek name of the plant giant-fennel. In building, it names the long arcaded porch that forms the entrance to a Christian church. The name may come from a fancied likeness to the reed-like plant.

To the narthex, learners in the faith and penitents were admitted. At times there was a second narthex, a vestibule inside the church. The outer one was then called the exonarthex. In Byzantine churches the inner narthex formed part of the main frame. A screen of columns divided it from the church proper. Some German churches also have a narthex. There it had no ritual meaning. It was used as a western transept, to give the west end more weight. The article points on to one of the finest examples of the form.
britannica-1911-pontifex:
Pontifex is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the most important priesthood of ancient Rome. The college of pontifices was charged with the part of civil law that dealt with the gods recognised by the state. It also held broad oversight of worship by clans and families. The name plainly comes from words for bridge and maker, though the entry says its first sense cannot now be fixed.

The article traces the college from the time of the kings, when it may have had three members who advised the king on religion. Under the republic it rose under a chief pontiff, the pontifex maximus. He took over the king's duties as head manager of religious law and lived in the regia, the house of the king.
britannica-1911-sussex:
Sussex, a county on the south coast of England, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Surrey bounds it on the north, Kent on the north-east, the English Channel on the south, and Hampshire on the west. It covers about 1,459 square miles. Its length from east to west is 78 miles, while its breadth never passes 28 miles.

The article gives most space to the shape of the land. A line of hills called the Forest Ridges forms the watershed and rises to about 800 feet near Crowborough. The South Downs run east for some 50 miles and end in the bold headland of Beachy Head near Eastbourne. North of the Downs lies the Weald. The Medway river rises in the county, and a small part of it drains toward the Thames.
britannica-1911-wessex:
Wessex is a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It tells of one of the kingdoms of early Saxon Britain. Old chronicle tales say two princes landed in the south and founded the realm. Their kin are said to have seized an island off the coast as well.

The entry tests those tales with care and finds weak points in them. Dates in the old books clash with each other, and some names look Welsh, not Saxon. Still, the growth of the realm under a later king is treated as real. His wins over Welsh foes won new land for the kingdom. The account shows how thin the proof is for the first kings of the south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-codex:
A codex is a manuscript book made from folded leaves. It replaced the older rolled scroll. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows the codex from its rise near the start of the fourth century. Parchment was the usual writing material. Papyrus was sometimes used too, despite its brittleness. Great Bible manuscripts survive in this form, and the entry groups the most famous of them for comparison.

Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Ephraemi stand as the four great codices of the Greek Bible. Codex Bezae joins them, prized for its unusual readings. Codex Amiatinus joins them too, as the greatest manuscript of the Latin Vulgate. Brief pointers send readers onward to the entry on Bible manuscripts. They also point to single famous books, such as the Book of Kells and the Book of Armagh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lex:
Lex, the Latin word for law, has a disputed etymology. Some trace it to Old Norse log. Others trace it to Latin legere. This article treats phrases beginning with lex or leges. In Roman use, lex plus a personal name, such as Lex Julia, meant a lex rogata. The magistrate put the law to the citizens, they declared acceptance, and it took the proposer's family name.

Imperial collections are called codices, bound as books. The title lex went to collections made by barbarian kings' order. When Teutonic tribes held imperial lands, the natives kept Roman law. For them Alaric II published in 506 the Lex Romana Wisigothorum, to cut the sources lawyers had to consult. This code held one year in Gaul, but lasted in Spain to the middle of the seventh century. It is also called Breviarium Alarici, after the referendary who signed its copies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-narthex:
A narthex, in early Christian architecture, is the west-end portion of a church, separated from the nave by a low wall or screen. It was reserved for catechumens, energumens and penitents not admitted among the congregation. The narthex came in two kinds, exterior and interior. The exterior was an open atrium arcade carried across the church front. The interior returned aisle and gallery across the nave.

Survivals stand at San Ambrogio in Milan for the exterior kind, and Santa Agnese in Rome for the interior. The outer narthex sometimes served as a hall of judgment and for secular uses, and after the sixth century as a burial place. The inner narthex, sometimes called the matroneum, likely served persons of rank rather than as a women's gallery. After the atrium faded in the West about 1000, the narthex grew into southern France's great west porch, then vanished with full Gothic.
charles-rex:
Ethel M. Dell published her novel in 1922, dedicating it with a poem about half-gods giving way to gods — courage, honour, faithfulness, and love. Lord Saltash opens the story bored on his yacht. Fed up with pleasure ashore, he orders Captain Larpent to sea tomorrow, and ennui sets the whole plot moving.

Four parts follow Saltash, the waif Toby, and the farming Boltons, Jake and Maud. Bunny, Larpent's daughter, and an ogre's castle of a great house fill the middle. A compact, a trap, and a confidence tighten the love story. Cards are played, a villain scores, and a turning-point comes late. Dell writes romance at full stretch, with Saltash's redemption as the prize.
doe-osti-2589328-small-scale-validation-:
National Energy Technology Laboratory report DOE/NETL-2025/4951, by William Fullmer, gathers bench-scale tests for checking a particle-flow simulation code. The code is MFIX-Exa, the laboratory's program for gas and solid flows such as fluidized beds, where gas lifts and stirs loose particles. The report was produced as output from an automated regression test using version 25.09 of the code.

Five published experiments anchor the checks, covering cold beds, a spouted bed, a mixed-size bed, a heated bed, and a bed that absorbs gas. With standard settings, a common drag model, and a standard heat transfer model, the code matched measured air gaps, particle speeds, temperature, and mixing fairly well. Engineers can use these cases to judge how much trust the code deserves on new designs.
doe-osti-2998770-collaborations-of-the-n:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/76, by Haomin Yuan, Dezhi Dai and Dillon Shaver, dated 30 September 2025, reviews a year of industry collaboration by the NEAMS Center of Excellence. The centre, launched in 2018, acts as a front door for firms that want to use NEAMS reactor simulation tools. It offers guidance, training and short joint projects on heat and fluid flow computing.

The fiscal 2025 partner was Kairos Power, a firm building a fluoride-salt-cooled pebble bed reactor. Joint work studied natural convection, where hot fluid rises on its own without pumps. One case cooled a canister of used fuel pebbles that still give off heat. The other modelled a reduced-width version of the Hermes test reactor core, with salt rising through heated pebbles and sinking through a cooled channel. The goal was heat-transfer values for both setups, with the study still under way.
doe-osti-3001540-tactical-analysis-for-c:
Kathryn Otte, Alysha Johnson, Ashley George and a PNNL team summarise TACCRAB in September 2025, an LDRD effort on risk at land borders. Screening pedestrians at a port of entry is a procedures problem: lanes, questions, secondary inspections. Each step changes the chance that a threat passes or an innocent traveller is delayed. TACCRAB, Tactical Analysis for Calculating Contextual Risk at Boundaries, turns those procedures into computable models.

Notional screening procedures were translated into graph format, so checkpoint designs could be compared with numbers, with boxplots of risk across configurations. Software pieces include a Mission Risk Simulator and an Attack Risk Calculator, with logged simulations and traveller profiles. Homeland Security operational views shaped the requirements over two years. Next steps point to cyber threat intelligence, sponsor data, open source data with machine learning, and reinforcement learning so the tool keeps improving. The report is the project's closing summary.
doe-osti-3021337-model-parameter-develop:
PNNL report by Erin I. Barker, Scott E. Muller, Floyd W. Hilty, and co-authors, dated January 2026, gauges how easily single chemical species hop through 316 stainless steel. Diffusion barriers set how fast steel corrodes and ages in reactors and chemical plants, but in a complex alloy each atom's local neighborhood changes its barrier. The team used systematic density functional theory runs to build species-specific values for modelers.

Of 400 planned runs spanning two compositions, twenty atomic arrangements, and ten defect types, 210 nudged elastic band runs survived screening across varied local chemical settings. Those runs yield diffusion barriers as distributions shaped by local chemistry, not single numbers. The statistical sampling strategy is itself a deliverable. It is a template for building defensible parameters for complex materials, where hand-picked structures would bias the answer.
doe-osti-3025747-annual-site-environment:
PanTeXas Deterrence, LLC prepared this annual site environmental report for the Pantex Plant near Amarillo, Texas, covering calendar year 2024 and issued in September 2025. The plant is the nation's nuclear weapons assembly and disassembly site, run for the National Nuclear Security Administration. The 198-page report is the plant's public environmental accounting: compliance status, monitoring results, and site conditions for the year.

Soil radioactivity sampling shows how quiet the results are. Uranium-234 and uranium-238 values at on-site, upwind, and downwind locations were statistically the same magnitude, so ground downwind of operations cannot be distinguished from background. The year's highest readings sat near the level of naturally occurring radioactive material in local soil. Relative maxima appeared both upwind and downwind, which points away from the plant as their source.
doe-osti-3363584-u-s-department-of-energ:
Yonghong Chen of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presents these February 2026 slides on the ENERGISE project, DOE's effort to enable extreme real-time grid integration of solar energy. The work, done with Southwest Power Pool, Polaris, and the Electric Power Research Institute, develops a multiday and intraday energy availability product for grid operators.

The design borrows option products from ISO New England, which pay generators a premium to arrange fuel in advance despite uncertainty about being called. Chen extends the idea across multiday reliability assessment and intraday commitment runs, where fuel arrangements and energy limited resources must be scheduled days ahead. A Southwest Power Pool case study works through the staging complexity.
doe-osti-3365145-ier-519-experiment-exec:
Los Alamos National Laboratory's report LA-UR-26-24128 documents experiment IER 519, called TEX Hanford, executed by Zach Lemke, Rene Sanchez, and Travis Grove. The experiment stacked iron-rich configurations, labeled Fe-11 and Fe-14, on the Planet critical assembly machine and measured when each stack went critical. Such benchmark data test the nuclear data and codes used to predict criticality safety.

Chapters give load sheets, reactor period measurements, and stack heights measured by coordinate measuring machine for each configuration. The Fe-14 stack was taken critical repeatedly, including after the safety rams dropped and were reinserted, and again on December 10, 2025 after sitting loaded overnight. Excess reactivity values cluster tightly across runs, around 8.4 to 8.7 cents in the later tables. The execution report preserves the raw record evaluators need.
doe-osti-3419432-probing-surface-hydrati:
Idaho poster INL/MIS-26-94597, dated August 2026, by Arthur Prewette, studies how proton-conducting ceramics take up water and swap isotopes. Wanhua Wang, Zeyu Zhao, and Dong Ding share the poster work. A custom DRIFTS cell watches surface chemistry at high heat during the swap.

Early exchange is fast at the surface, then slows as deuterons move into the bulk. Hydroxyl groups refill at the surface, causing a lag in signal loss. Those steps matter, since surface hydroxyls drive proton conduction. Fuel cell and sensor teams learn which step limits the whole process.
eeldrop-and-appleplex:
Eeldrop and Appleplex, by T S Eliot, is a short prose sketch of two men who rent rooms in a disreputable street and mostly talk. Eliot explains that they chose the neighborhood with care. Evil streets of noise exist, and evil streets of silence. His pair preferred the silence, under a cloud of respectability with something to conceal. Their windows face the entrance of a police station, which delights them.

Whenever an arrest breaks the quiet, the street fills with dressing gowns and caps, and the two rush out to mingle. Appleplex, gifted with an easy address among the lower classes, questions onlookers and collects full and inconsistent histories. Eeldrop listens and observes. Written before Eliot's fame as a poet, the piece shows his early method already formed: the city at night, talk as action, and meaning gathered from what bystanders cannot agree on.
elizabeth-and-essex:
Lytton Strachey calls his 1928 life of Elizabeth and Essex a tragic history. He gives the book to Alix and James Strachey. Seventeen chapters trace the old queen and the young earl. The first chapter sets the stage wide. The English Reformation, he argues, was a social revolution as much as a religious one. A new class of Cecils and Russells took the reins of power.

Essex, Robert Devereux, flares up in that settled world. He stands as the last spirit of feudal chivalry. Strachey stages famous scenes with a novelist's hand. The queen, ambushed by a Latin speech, rounds on her courtiers with a smile. By God's death, she cries, she has been forced to scour up her old Latin, long rusting. She wishes aloud that Essex had heard it. Their love, pride, and ruin drive the book to its scaffold end.
govdocs-archive_org-gravity_high_strange: An index rather than a readable work, this file lists damaged and partially legible government document pages on UAP, antigravity, and what researchers call high strangeness. The entries were assembled from folio sheets marked with archival-action fields, the bookkeeping of a records release. As a finding aid, it shows the shape of the underlying file even where the pages themselves can no longer be read.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DavisonAlexisHD: Only a fragment survives of an FBI airtel sent between the Bureau's Dallas and Denver offices about the Davison family. The fragment names Mrs. Hal Davison of Atlanta, Georgia. Its full subject and context are not recoverable from what remains, so the record documents the Bureau's interest in the family without explaining the reason behind it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Permindex_Permi: Jeffrey Steinberg and David Goldman wrote about Permindex under a striking title: 'Permindex: Britain's International Assassination Bureau.' Permindex was a trade organization that Jim Garrison's inquiry linked to the Kennedy assassination. The article presents the group's British connections as an assassination bureau. The file gives the authors and the title. It does not preserve the article's evidence, so its charges are reported here as its framing, not as findings.
harvard-psychological-studies-volume-1-c:
The first volume of the Harvard Psychological Studies gathers sixteen experimental investigations from the Harvard Psychological Laboratory. It appeared as a monograph supplement of The Psychological Review, the journal edited by J. McKeen Cattell and J. Mark Baldwin. Hugo Münsterberg, Harvard's professor, stands among the cooperating editors, with names such as Alfred Binet, John Dewey, and Joseph Jastrow. The laboratory at Harvard was then the most famous in America.

The papers report bench work of the new science: tests of sensation, memory, attention, and feeling, with apparatus, tables, and exact counts. Psychology was splitting from philosophy in these years, and this volume is the split in print. The prose is technical and the topics narrow by design. For the history of the science, the book is a landmark: American experimental psychology showing its first full set of results.
nasa-tm-19700017991-ephemeris-of-a-highl:
Barbara E. Lowrey of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in May 1970. It gives an ephemeris for Explorer 28, also called IMP 3, a satellite in a highly eccentric orbit. An ephemeris is a table that lists where an object will be at set times.

Lowrey's ephemeris matched two years of radio observations well and stayed close to optical observations a year later. It was built by numerical integration from launch conditions, with no later correction passes. She improved the starting conditions by matching computed perigee times against observed ones. Because such orbits are hard to compute, the long matched arc can serve as a standard for other work.
sex-and-society-studies-in-the-social-ps:
William I. Thomas, associate professor of sociology at the University of Chicago, gathered these studies in 1907; a fourth impression followed in 1913. The pieces first ran in journals at scattered dates. Thomas revised and in places expanded them for the book, by request of readers who found them hard to reach.

One thesis runs through the set: bodily habits differ by sex, with men stronger, more restless, and more apt for motion, women more settled. Thomas traces how that gap shaped social forms, work, morals, and mind. Studies treat early social control, early industry, modesty, and related themes in turn.
the-descent-of-man-and-selection-in-rela:
Charles Darwin's The Descent of Man and Selection in Relation to Sex is laid out in three parts. Part I treats the descent or origin of man, the proof of his rise from some lower form. It compares his mental powers with those of lower animals, and treats the races of man. Parts II and III turn to sexual selection, tracing secondary sexual characters in insects, fishes, birds, and mammals, and then in man himself.

A preface to the second edition explains that, through the reprints of the first edition, published in 1871, Darwin was able to introduce several important corrections. With more time passed, he has now profited by the fiery ordeal the book went through, taking up every criticism that seems to him sound. Many correspondents, he adds, sent a surprising store of new facts and remarks, of which he could use only the more important.
the-discovery-of-yellowstone-park-journa:
Nathaniel Pitt Langford's The Discovery of Yellowstone Park, dated 1905, presents his journal of the Washburn Expedition to the Yellowstone and Firehole Rivers in the year 1870. A contents note lists a foreword and index not included here. A portrait of James Bridger stands near the front.

Langford opens on the mountaineers of Montana, reputed fabricators who loved practicing on the credulity of their listeners. Bridger, discoverer of Great Salt Lake, wove so much romance around his Indian adventures that hearers took them with many grains of allowance. Once, near Pumpkin Butte by Fort Laramie, a young attache asked if he had lived long on the plains. Bridger pointed at the butte, a thousand feet above the plain, and said that mountain was a hole in the ground when he came here. Bridger's mountain life began in 1820, and by 1832 he was a resident partner in the Rocky Mountain Fur Company.
the-spectator-volumes-1-2-and-3-with-tra: Henry Morley's edition of The Spectator, in three volumes and dated 1891, presents the same front matter found in the separate volume-one record. It shows the title page promising the text as first printed, with the authors' own corrections, plus notes and an index. A publisher's advertisement and a stretch of verse follow. The essays themselves do not appear in the pages present here.
three-contributions-to-the-theory-of-sex: Prof. Sigmund Freud's Three Contributions to the Theory of Sex appears as number seven in a nervous and mental disease monograph series. A. A. Brill translated it, and James J. Putnam wrote the introduction. The Nervous and Mental Disease Publishing Company issued this second edition reprinting at New York and Washington in 1920. A series list names works by White, Jung, Plaut, and Freud himself on hysteria. The opening pages give credits and the series catalogue only, so Freud's three essays themselves are not shown in this record.
